subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this debate adjourned on February 2 I had halfway concluded my remarks. Perhaps it would be useful at this point, since the debate is now being resumed after three weeks, if I were to commence by repeating the suggested amendment that has been placed on the record by my colleague, the hon. member for Flamilton West (Mr. Alexander), which of course will be moved on behalf of the official opposition when this bill goes to committee. The amendment is as follows:
In high unemployment regions, the minister may, with the approval of the governor in council, make regulations
-lowering from 12 weeks down to a minimum of 8 weeks the number of
weeks referred to in subsection 16(1) and 17(2)(a)
-defining high unemployment regions, delineating the boundaries thereof
and determining residence and eligibility within such region;
-setting a date of termination for any such regulations-
Mr. Speaker, I hope my hon. friend from New Brunswick who is interrupting me will support the amendment because it is very important to northern New Brunswick. This bill will affect northern New Brunswick as much or probably even more than my own province of Newfoundland.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I only have limited time I will gladly accept a question from the hon. member at the end of my speech.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: You would change your whole speech if you listened to him.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Again, the hon. member from New Brunswick who interrupts should support our amendment which could change the whole course of this bill. I do not see how any member from the Atlantic provinces cannot support the amendment. Unemployment in northern New Brunswick is among the highest in the country and will take a great deal of explaining by the hon. member, more than I suspect he is capable of.
I am glad to know there is concern, as was exemplified by the interjections at the commencement of my remarks by my learned and friendly colleague from New Brunswick. That province is on record as having the second highest unemployment rate in the country-second to my own province. When you get into the northern part of New Brunswick-where the hon. gentleman who continues to interrupt me comes from- then, of course, the unemployment rate is as bad and in some cases is worse than it is in Newfoundland.
Since the debate adjourned on February 2-and perhaps I should underline and emphasize again the importance of this bill-the latest figures have been issued by Statistics Canada referring to unemployment for the month of January. One thing we can draw from those figures is that if we needed
[Mr. Goodale.)
proof, it is obviously here, that the present method of measuring unemployment by Statistics Canada is, to say at least, grossly inadequate. I have referred to the seriousness of that already. It is based on these figures released monthly by Statistics Canada that allocations are made for the government's make-work programs such as the Local Initiatives Program, the Canada Works program and Young Canada Works program.
If we examine the figures for the month of January we find that on a seasonally adjusted basis the figures for Newfoundland were 13.6 per cent, representing a decline of two decimal points from 13.8 per cent from the previous month. Of course, taking into account the seasonally adjusted figures, more people were reported unemployed for the month of January than for the previous month.
The same situation applies to the national figures for the month of January which places unemployment in Canada, on a seasonally adjusted basis, at 7.5 per cent compared to the same figure for the previous month of December. Yet for the month of January we reached an all-time record. There were more people out of work in Canada in the month of January than in the history of this country since records have been kept. That fact was brought out quite forcibly in an article which appeared in the February 12 edition of the Toronto Star. It listed figures that had been leaked by someone in Statistics Canada showing the real rate of unemployment in Canada for the previous year, 1976.
According to these figures, the official unemployment rate in the province of Newfoundland in 1976 was 14.7 per cent, and officially represented 25,000 people. But there are others who were not regarded by this new methodology of Statistics Canada which was adopted a year ago, and they represent another 28,000 unemployed unreported in the statistics, for a total of 53,000 unemployed, or 25 per cent. There is obviously something wrong with our method of measurement.
Let us look at the methodology for the country as a whole, using the same figures. In Canada as a whole, the rate for 1976 was 7.1 per cent, representing in official terms 735,000 Canadians. But another 450,000 people in the country never qualified to be reported in these statistics: these are the hidden unemployed, the unemployable, the unemployed unemployables. These are the people who have given up, who have been on the labour market for so long that they had given up looking for work, either for lack of skill, surplus in a particular skill or through sheer frustration at their inability to find work. That brings the total unemployed in Canada to 1,185,000, or 11 per cent. Yet officially-and these are the figures on which the government bases its programs-the figure was 7.1 per cent, or 735,000 people unemployed for the year.
Let us look at the method of measuring unemployment. I refer to a document released by Statistics Canada last February to explain the new methodology, entitled "Conceptual, Definitional and Methodological Changes in the Labour Force Survey". Under the heading "Methodology" it reads:
Except for the new questionnaire design, the methodology used is obtaining labour force survey data is similar in the LFS and RLFS. However, the revised
February 25, 1977

survey has introduced a number of refinements and some of the more important improvements will be presented in this section.
LFS is "labour force survey" and I presume RLFS is "revised labour force survey". The document goes on to define some of those refinements. At page 3 it reads:
Finally, persons not in the labour force are those who are unwilling or unable, during reference week, to supply labour services under existing labour market conditions.
Obviously, half the total of the unemployed fall into that category. Then we go to the end of the document and find this statement in the summary.
-more precise measures of employment and unemployment and the generation of additional information-
Finally the document reads:
When taken in conjunction with the additional information collected about persons who are classified as not in the labour force, the data users-
Those are people who go into the field one week out of four to gather this information.
-can, and in fact are encouraged to, formulate definitions of unemployment which are best suited to their particular applications.
I suggest this puts far too much discretion in the hands of surveyors, the people who actually gather the data. There is ample evidence of the correctness of my contention. According to Statistics Canada, 29,000 were unemployed in my province in January. However, on checking with the Unemployment Insurance Commission I discovered that in that same month, January, there were 60,000 drawing unemployment insurance benefits-60,000 out of a total work force of 168,000 persons.
You can only qualify for unemployment insurance if you are available for work; availability for work is a prerequisite qualification for the receipt of unemployment insurance benefits. If you are available for work, you must be in the work force. Clearly, therefore, the unemployment figures for Newfoundland and for Canada as a whole are misleading. They do not show how serious is the unemployment situation in this country. That is also why I question the judgment-indeed, the humanity-of the government in bringing forward this bill at this time.
I do not deny that the bill contains some excellent features. Obviously, the move to combine the functions of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the department of manpower is long overdue since those two services are complementary. But if the bill passes it will eliminate many Canadians from the unemployment rolls and force them onto the welfare rolls of the provinces. This is not the time to do it. Although this bill may represent a reform, and even though, as my colleague from Hamilton said, it would provide more incentives to work or more disincentives to not work, I submit this is not the time to bring forward the particular amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act embodied in this bill.
The C. D. Howe Research Institute, in a policy paper entitled "New Directions for Manpower Policy" which was released on November 1, 1976, said in part:
Employment and Immigration
The government's main response to cyclical unemployment should continue to be unemployment insurance and fiscal and monetary policies.
I note the words "should continue to be unemployment insurance and fiscal and monetary policies." The C. D. Howe Research Institute is a well respected and highly regarded institute or "think tank", if you like. I quoted the research institute to support my argument, namely, that this is not the time, during a period of critically high unemployment, to tamper with the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
I am glad my hon. friend agrees. I knew he would because he is genuinely concerned, as I am about the present situation. He, too, comes from one of the Atlantic provinces. Let us consider the effects of this bill. Who will be affected by the provision changing the qualifying period from 8 to 12 weeks? I shall put forward the figures pertaining to my own province. My hon. friend opposite can refer to the figures relating to New Brunswick. Mr. Speaker, my province will be hardest hit because we have the highest rate of unemployment in the country by far. Bear in mind, Mr. Speaker, that 74 per cent of all those affected are male. When you consider that 44 per cent of that group are 25 years old and older, it is obvious that families will be hardest hit because the heads of families will be disqualified from unemployment insurance benefits. I say that, sir, notwithstanding the assurances given in June by the minister's predecessor who said that these reforms would affect, basically, only students and housewives. The fact that heads of families in my province will be hardest hit gives the lie to that statement.
As I have already said, the burden will fall heavily on the low income earner. Let me illustrate. In Newfoundland, 45 per cent of those affected earn less than $90 a week and 30 per cent of the group affected earn up to $129 a week. What do those figures tell you? If you earn $90 a week, it means that you can draw up to $60 per week in benefits.
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult enough to live on $90 a week anywhere in Canada, especially in my province where the cost of living is high. Surely it is nigh impossible to live on unemployment insurance of $60 a week. I say this to give the lie to those who charge that we must get people off unemployment insurance. Canadians do not, by and large, draw unemployment insurance from choice. They draw unemployment insurance because they cannot find work. They must fall back on unemployment insurance as a means of supporting their families.
Taking people off the unemployment insurance rolls will do something else in the hardest pressed provinces where unemployment is highest. It will place an additional, heavy financial burden on those provinces, especially Newfoundland. At present, people can qualify for unemployment insurance benefits after eight weeks of work. But if they are taken off the unemployment insurance rolls or disqualified they will fall back on our welfare system. At least half of welfare payments must be financed by the province under the Canada Assistance Plan. It is estimated that if this bill passes Newfoundland this
80010-11%

February 25, 1977
Employment and Immigration
year will have to bear an additional 16 per cent increase in the cost of welfare benefits.
My colleague from Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) talked about the seasonality of work in the Atlantic provinces. Seasonal jobs are a fact of life in many parts of Canada, certainly in the Atlantic provinces. Bear in mind that work projects under the government's Local Initiatives Program usually last about two months. I do not think that is coincidental. I think such programs have been geared to last that long in order to enable those who would otherwise or normally be unemployed with work for a long enough period to qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. Until such make-work programs are phased out-in other words, until we reach a situation in which there is full employment or almost full employment which might be based upon an unemployment rate of 4 per cent or less-I do not think we should tamper with the Unemployment Insurance Act. I say this because at present our make-work programs are geared to the existing provisions of the act.
Obviously, we need a comprehensive employment strategy in this country. We have heard talk in the Atlantic provinces of such a strategy for a number of years. For the last six or seven years the DREE program has been available to us. The DREE program was to be the be-all and end-all of the fight against high unemployment in the high unemployment areas of the country. Unfortunately, the DREE program was not productive. That is to say, it was not successful because as a program it operated in almost total isolation from other government policies. It operated in isolation from monetary and fiscal policies, transportation policies and the government's own tariff policies.
Also, it was necessary to consider all those policies in order to formulate a comprehensive employment strategy. After all, there is not much point in offering industry DREE grants to locate in the Atlantic provinces, on the one hand, and increasing freight rates on the other. One policy, obviously, is counter productive with respect to the other. Until this country has a job strategy or an employment strategy we shall continue to be plagued with high unemployment-and when we have high unemployment in Canada as a whole we have critically high unemployment in the eastern regions of Canada.
There is one other thing we should bear in mind. In the past number of years, going back as far as I can remember in this House-in fact, ever since fishermen were included as qualifying for unemployment insurance in 1956-we have been promised a special income stabilization program for fishermen. The Gill report, which was the last major study into the Unemployment Insurance Act in 1970, had this to say:
Income stabilization is imperative in the commercial fisheries, with particular reference to the remoter fishing communities, and, pending the completion of plans being prepared specifically for this purpose, self-employed fishermen will be covered by unemployment insurance.
That obviously referred to plans which were under way at that time. In the election of June, 1974, in a speech at Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau)

said, and I quote from "Notes for remarks by the Prime Minister-Liberal party policy on fisheries, June 21, 1974":
And, of great importance to fishermen and their families, we are committed to bring in an income stabilization plan to ensure a reasonable average level of earnings.
I appeal to my colleagues opposite from the Atlantic provinces who come from areas where there is heavy dependence upon the fishing industry, where fishing is a major economic factor, not to proceed with this amendment to the act at this time. Withdraw this amendment until the government brings in its promised and "long under development" income stabilization program for fishermen. Otherwise this amendment which changes the qualifying period from eight to 12 weeks will not only hit hardest the heads of families and low income earners in this country but it will hit also hardest the fishermen, the plant workers, the seasonal operations in this country, whether it is processing, packing, fishing for lobster in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, or the more seasonal fishing operations of the northeast coast of Newfoundland where you can only fish for a short period of time. The produce of that very short fishery has to be processed in less than 12 weeks.
All the people in these seasonal fishing operations in the Atlantic provinces, the Magdalen Islands and the eastern part of Quebec, will be disqualified from drawing unemployment insurance. Given the seasonal nature of their work and the limitation of employment opportunities in these regions, they will have no choice but to fall back on the welfare rolls of these provinces. They are proud people. They should not have to go on welfare. These provinces should not have to add to their already overburdened welfare rolls at this time in our history.

For this reason I am concerned about this 12-week landmark that the government has established for all parts of Canada. We frequently hear it said that regions of Canada are affected by various problems and for that reason we should have flexible federalism. I am not suggesting that we need flexible federalism or a balanced federalism, but that federal government programs should be sufficiently flexible to take account of the circumstances obtaining in various regions of the country.

I realize we do not like giving the governor in council discretionary powers, but we must consider human problems in the various regions of this country. Therefore, I think the best solution is to exercise discretion in favour of people in depressed areas.
If the government carries out all the programs it has announced to improve the employment situation, this particular problem may disappear and we will not have to designate certain regions for special attention in terms of lowering the 12-week period to eight weeks. The province of Ontario could not get the federal government to commit itself, and Finally the province had to act on its

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. Just prior to the lunch break I tried to bring my thoughts on the topic of Bill C-27 to the attention of the House in dealing with the government's bill to try to make minimum benefits payable only to a person who works for 12 weeks. The amendment which our party has suggested is that in special circumstances, when humanitarian concerns are most evident in places of high unemployment, this period could perhaps be reduced down to as low as eight weeks.
I also tried to indicate that some concerns about unemployment insurance, some of which are being dealt with under this legislation, were first raised in the 1972 election campaign. A bill on the order paper of the twenty-ninth parliament died on the order paper, and have had to wait 4'/2 years for the government to take any action.
I want for a moment to deal with what is perhaps the major unemployment problem in Canada, which is youth unemployment. Today in Canada 46 per cent of the people who are on the unemployment insurance rolls are between age 14 and 24. This is absolutely ridiculous. It is unfair to an age group which is offering so much to this country and which wants to offer so much to this country that they are the ones who are being denied an opportunity to make the contribution they wish to make.
As somebody once indicated, the logic of Manpower's approach toward unemployment in Canada affecting those between 14 and 24 years of age was obscured by the growth of Manpower's many programs. That person indicated that the program failures were always being met by band-aid remedies. We have a perfect example of some of these band-aid remedies. Last year, prior to Christmas, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) announced two "brilliant" new programs for the creation of jobs. They were really going to do wonders for the Canadian economy. He announced the Canada Works program and the Young Canada Works program. He announced that they were going to be five-year programs. I suppose if one were skeptical about it, one would assume that the government believes it is going to be so inefficient over the next few years that it requires these make-work programs to be in place for five years to get over the government's ineptness. However, the young people in Canada, the people between 14 and 24 who make up half the unemployed, have been given a special program-the Young Canada Works Program-and as we see from a Manpower advertisement, it is geared generally to students who will work on community benefit programs which will enable them to test their career aspirations.
If we read further we find that students can expect six weeks of consecutive work. I am sure that in those six weeks the
February 25, 1977

students will be able to discover all the facets of their career aspirations! It goes on to say that the program can work up to 14 weeks. So between a 6-week and a 14-week period the department of manpower believes young people in the age group between 14 and 24 will find jobs which will help them in their career aspirations.
This is just ludicrous. Maybe they are creating jobs, but they are certainly not creating jobs which will help people generally in their careers. First of all, they are restricting the jobs to community benefits. In other advertising it is indicated that work will be created by a community group, a group responsible in the community, perhaps a municipal council. It is just another band-aid. It will generate some jobs like Opportunities for Youth. In the past we have had LIP, which closely resembles Canada Works, but this is only a band-aid approach and a scratch on the surface.
Also, we are going to have, as indicated in answer to a question I asked the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), a department responsible for a program which may become entitled "operation Canada". Indications that I have are that it will be under the Minister of National Defence. The minister submitted to cabinet on December 1 a plan for "operation Canada" which will bring Canadians between the ages of 17 and 22 together for a ten months' period. This "operation Canada" program is to demonstrate that through physical development, mental fitness and the resilience of Canadian youth, they will provide a greater service to the Canadian nation. They plan to start on a pilot program involving about 1,000 people in this youth corps, and it will cost in the beginning about $5,145,000, or a little over $5,000 per person for the ten months during which they will be employed. That program might start in July, 1977, and they hope they will have 10,000 participants involved by January 1978, with a budget of about $48 million.
I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question about this youth corps about a week ago and he said about the program-which was mentioned in the throne speech-that he did not know when it would be enacted or under which department it would come, but it would be introduced in the second half of this session. It appears to me that the government threw the idea into the throne speech without thinking it out. Now, some five months later, they are trying to think a bit more about it. They will set it up under the Minister of National Defence. I do not know whether it will be a paramilitary group in the outbound movement mode, as the Minister of National Defence expressed it. Perhaps they will even teach them the proper and safe use of firearms; I do not know. There is to be an option whereby people working in the youth corps will have an opportunity of joining the forces.
I am very interested in this program but I am not sure how it will help the youth in this country, who are underemployed right now, to meet their career aspirations, unless one considers the limited number of people who may have career aspirations in the military or who do not know what they are going
Employment and Immigration
to do and take ten months to work in this paramilitary group, this youth corps, the establishment of which was announced but on which the government cannot give us any figures or any specifics. Again, this is a band-aid approach. We do not know whether in this youth corps the young people will be taught any life skills or career skills. They will be taught how to get along with their neighbours and how to get along in the outdoors, as far as we know.
This program, along with Young Canada Works program, does not attack the real problem of future unemployment in this country. Canada Works, which is much like LIP, will not attack the real unemployment problems in this country because under the Canada Works program they are accepting applications for bits and pieces of work which some organizations would like to sponsor, and which will benefit communities, which would normally be of 32 weeks' duration but may be extended to up to 52 weeks. So, again, it is a temporary program. A person cannot find a career job in any one of these government band-aid programs.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), prior to Christmas, in a paper which he put forth announced the Young Canada Works and Canada Works programs and went on to say how much help they would be to help students at universities find career opportunities. At that time I believe there were 72 Manpower offices located on university or post-secondary institution campuses. He announced that he would increase that number by another 17 so that there would be about 89 Manpower offices on the campuses of secondary institutions.
It is strange that the government keeps spending money in this way when the return it is getting is so limited. One of the major universities in Ontario carried out a survey of their student population who had graduated and left university, to see how many of them found jobs through Manpower offices. They found that some 9 per cent of the graduate students had found jobs through Manpower offices. They were, basically, people who did not know what they wanted to do and had taken a construction job or another hourly or weekly paid job through the student Manpower office. After another nine months, that figure went down to a little over 5 per cent of the students who obtained their jobs through a Manpower office.
Expanding the Manpower network on university campuses may not be a wise expenditure of money, because obviously the vast majority of students do not find the Manpower office to be the place to go when looking for a job. Indeed, the experience in my riding is that even people who want an hourly or weekly paid job do not go to the Manpower office to look for it. Also, people who have real career aspirations, whether it be in business, in law or in any other career option which a person may have by getting post-secondary education, do not generally leave it to the Manpower office on their local campus to find them a job. Usually they get a job through their own initiative, or perhaps even by going to one of the specialized personnel agencies which hire for executive, management training jobs or sales jobs.

February 25, 1977
Employment and Immigration
To show that the Department of Manpower and Immigration is rather contradictory in its approach, let me point out that the figures on youth unemployment are a scandal. They are the highest Canada has ever had, in absolute terms- meaning in the number of unemployed-and in percentage terms, since the department started collecting special data on youth unemployment in 1952. Oddly enough, last year, in spite of this the Department of Manpower and Immigration withdrew the budget for collecting student unemployment data. Since the 1950s the department, in co-ordination with Statistics Canada, has always done, in the months of May, June, July, August and September, special student unemployment surveys in which they have asked whether the person was a student in the preceding month of March, whether the person was looking for summer employment now, and whether the person intended being a student the following September. By this series of questions they could isolate who was really a student and intended to continue his studies and thus could put an actual figure on student unemployment.
Last year the government, in its wisdom, decided to withdraw the small budget-which I think amounted to around $12,000-to carry out these surveys and instead incorporated in its general survey questions which initially they said would indicate student unemployment. They asked, "Were you a student last week? Are you a student now? Will you be a student next week?" Of course, if the person was asked in the last week of July whether he had been a student the previous week, his answer was "No", because the institution had closed in May. To the question whether he was going to be a student the following week, the first of August, the answer, of course, was "No", because the institution would not open until September. So, naturally, they did not get the correct Figures for youth student unemployment. It was a neat little trick, and rather deceitful. It did not give the government the correct statistical base to plan appropriately for students entering the work force in the years ahead.
[DOT] (M20)
I was very pleased to hear that as a result of a condemnation by this party, other parties and members of this House, the department has rethought this shortsighted policy. As a result of questions asked by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) in the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, the minister indicated that he would reinstitute student employment surveys this coming summer. I think that is part of a program which may be more helpful than the rather shortsighted programs the government has used in the past. At least it will provide some statistical base for dealing with some of the youth unemployment in this country.
The government should concentrate on this problem and really do something to try to find employment for the young people of this country. As chairman of the Progressive Conservative caucus committee on youth, I have tried over the last number of months to get to many youth conferences, to a number of universities and to other places where young people gather, to try to find out what they want the federal govern-

ment to provide. I have found out, from the limited exposure I have had, that they do not want more OFY, Young Canada Works or LIP-type opportunities.
Young people laugh, they say that these programs are a rip-off and that they are a waste of taxpayers' money, but if the government is going to be so stupid as to give it out this way, they might as well take their share of it. I suppose that is a reasonable attitude to take, but these young people really want career opportunities, full-time jobs, jobs in which there is an opportunity for advancement. They want jobs which they believe contribute to Canadian society as a whole. They want jobs which they see as being productive and helpful. When I say "productive", I do not mean working on an assembly line and increasing the output of canned meats from 19,000 cans per hour to 22,000 cans per hour. They want to be productive by doing something which will help society.
In my university days, back in the late fifties and early sixties, the attitude was that we wanted jobs which paid high salaries. There were all kinds of people around recruiting in universities at that time. In the late sixties and early seventies people took time off, travelled, bummed around and had experiences, but not working experiences. Students today have returned to some extent to the approach taken in the late fifties and early sixties. They want serious jobs, jobs with career opportunities and jobs which are socially useful to Canadian society as a whole. They want jobs which are meaningful to them, but perhaps they are influenced by that other era of the late sixties and early seventies in that they are not necessarily demanding high-paying jobs. Perhaps they would take a job which pays $12,000 rather than $15,000 if they felt the environment in that lower-paying job was more appropriate to them.
They may be more selective in that they might like to work in a small town or for a small company rather than for a large, multinational company or in a large city. They are more selective with regard to the environment and the type of job, than they are with regard to the dollar value attributed to the job. This is the kind of thing the young people of this country want. They do not want band-aid programs, although they will take advantage of them while they are still around and while the government tries to rely on them. However, this government will not substantially improve the climate for these students until it tackles the real job, and that is the job of expanding business in this country and expanding business opportunities so that business can grow and will require more employees in full-time jobs.
I feel that the government has let down Canadian society as a whole-and this is one of the reasons for the quarrelling and grumbling of today-because it has not approached business in Canada in an enlightened way which would encourage business to expand. For example, in the textile industry we find that in the United States 85 per cent of the textiles sold are produced there. In the European Economic Community, 90 per cent of the textiles used there are made in that community.
What has our government allowed this country to do? Only 45 per cent of the textiles used in Canada are made here.
February 25, 1977

Because of our do-gooder attitude, our Boy Scout attitude, and as a result of GATT negotiations, we have lowered our tariffs and our quotas on imports. This has wiped out thousands of jobs in this country. It has been estimated that in the textile industry alone, if we could come back up to 75 per cent or 80 per cent fabrication in this country almost 200,000 more jobs would be created. As anybody who follows the textile industry would know, we have been closing down textile plants at an alarming rate, so much so that finally last fall the government, through political considerations or finally just seeing its folly, realized the problem and just prior to the completion of the Quebec election campaign the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) announced quotas on imported textiles.
I am sure that was not motivated by political considerations any more than the announcement a week before provincial by-elections that the Department of Veterans Affairs was moving to Prince Edward Island, or any more than the announcement in Prince Albert last week that there would be a new transportation policy affecting that area. That announcement is prior to two by-elections taking place in Saskatchewan next Tuesday. 1 would not have thought the government would come out with these goodies in provinces where by-elections are taking place, just for political reasons; but I was very pleased to see that the government finally, for whatever reason, decided to put a quota on some textile imports. Hopefully, over the next few years we will be able to re-establish that industry, create more jobs, take some of the people who are presently unemployed off the unemployment rolls and put them back into useful, productive jobs.
The knowledge the federal government had that it was going to close down the textile industry goes back to the late sixties and early seventies, because in 1970 the federal government introduced legislation-actually, by order in council, the Appropriations Act No. 4 of 1970-and regulations to benefit clothing and textile workers. It was updated in 1974. This legislation provides a form of pension plan under the unemployment insurance scheme for people who are in the textile industry which the government was in the process of closing down across the country because of its do-gooder policy. There were jobs there which would have taken youthful Canadians off the unemployment rolls.
In the electronics industry the government is doing the very same thing, because in our negotiations at GATT Canada said it would abide by those GATT agreements and allow underprivileged and underdeveloped countries to export into Canada duty-free. Now it appears that because of diminishing trade in the television industry we have lost 20,000 jobs in the electronics industry since 1973. As a matter of fact I can give substance to that, Mr. Speaker. RCA had a plant in Renfrew, Ontario, which in 1972 provided 440 jobs. By 1974, that plant was down to 240 jobs as a result of the government's Bill C-170 in the twenty-ninth parliament which gave benefits to the so-called underdeveloped and underprivileged countries. That plant is now closed. There are no jobs whatsoever. That is
Employment and Immigration
an example of where 440 jobs in my constituency are a part of the 20,000 lost by the television industry in the last few years.
There are other areas which show the government is making a mistake and is not pursuing an intelligent policy of full employment. In my constituency there is the only magnesium mine in Canada. It has a capacity of over 10,000 metric tons per year, and in 1968 was producing at capacity. As a result of this government's policies it is now producing only 4,000 metric tons, or a little over 40 per cent of capacity, annually. But imports of magnesium have gone from 2,000 metric tons in 1968 to 8,000 metric tons today. This is not because it is a rotten, "no good" facility-it may be all of that, or none of that-but in 1968 Canada had a 17 percent tariff and in 1975 it had a 5 per cent tariff. The United States has a 20 cent tariff on magnesium imports. The European Economic Community, which does not have any mines, has a 9 per cent tariff; and the Japanese, who have perhaps the most sensible program, have a 15 per cent tariff on imported magnesium until all domestic magnesium is used up. The Boy Scouts of this government go out saying that we will have the lowest tariff nation in the world, and to hang with the jobs. Well, we have lowered ours to one of the lowest, weak groups-5 per cent, and we are now importing more than ever before.
Mr. Speaker, the saddest example of government bungling in the last few years concerns a plant which wanted to employ 80 people. It applied to Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in 1974 to set up scissors manufacturing in Canada. Canada has never manufactured scissors. The department said it was a brillant idea and made a report showing how well it could be done. Based on that and other considerations, the company went ahead, and largely through an Ontario Development Corporation loan of almost $500,000 built a modern, efficient plant to produce hot, forged steel scissors in Canada. But then this government passed the infamous bill allowing imports from countries, so-called developing or underdeveloped, into Canada duty-free. Now scissors are flooding into this country from Brazil and this company cannot employ the 80 people it wanted to employ. They only employ 25 and are having to diversify-so we have lost 55 jobs there. At the same time, we certainly get equal treatment from Brazil; their tariff on imported scissors was 150 per cent, but it was changed a few months ago to total prohibition. If we are to provide business opportunities in this country, we must have a more constant approach-
