subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us deals with changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act, but it is significant in not only what it does about the unemployed who seek benefits but also as a statement of the government's employment policy or lack thereof. I should like to spend a few minutes looking at the issue of unemployment and then relate that to the bill before us, making a few specific criticisms. I will then put forward what I hope are some constructive counterproposals on the question of getting Canadians back to work.
What worries me is the sense of complacency, almost, among the general public that unemployment is a natural state in Canada and that somehow we have to accept high unemployment as inevitable. It is shocking that today there are more people out of work than at the height of the great depression in the 1930s; yet we do not see mass marches of the unemployed and letters to the editor and the media taking up the cause of this great human crisis.
It is argued that is because the benefits we give to the unemployed are adequate to carry them through. That may or may not be correct, as the individual case would tell. Beyond that, however, is the fact that Canadians have come to accept the lack of solution by both the old line parties, Liberals and Conservatives, to solving the problem and have accepted the situation as just the state of the Canadian economy from which we will extricate ourselves. I reject that kind of complacency. I think that when we have over 800,000 Canadians out of work according to the official statistics, and when we take into account the hidden unemployed-those not measured by Statistics Canada because they have tried week after week to find work and have given up the search-the unemployment figure is closer to one million Canadians.
The cost, both in human and economic terms, is devastating. How demoralizing it must be for a young worker with a family to support to find that no matter how hard he tries he cannot find employment. Think of the emotional stress this must place on him and his young family and the kind of marital problems it could bring. It is something that those of us who have jobs all too easily forget.
From workers in the electrical industry who presented a brief to the New Democratic Party labour committee only yesterday we hear of lay-offs in General Electric and Westing-house ranging from between 35 per cent to 50 per cent of the work force. You cannot tell me that those working people accept a situation like that calmly and will act as if nothing has happened. Those laid off, those unemployed for many months, have little chance of finding another job if the jobs are not there to be found.
At present in this country we have about 40,000 job vacancies and one million people unemployed. No matter how much
(Mr. Dick.]
you try to shift workers around, no matter how much you try to move the unemployed to areas in which there are jobs, you will still face an immense shortfall in the number of jobs available. Surely the government and we, as parliamentarians, should be concerned about the cost of unemployment in human terms, the erosion of self-dignity and the work ethic.
This government is not proposing massive solutions for curing unemployment-unemployment which is exacting a great toll from Canadian workers in human terms. Nor does the government really know what high unemployment year after year costs our economy. It seems to me that most Canadians do not realize that unemployment costs our economy billions of dollars worth of goods which are not produced. Unemployment costs the Canadian taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars in extra taxes needed to supplement the unemployment insurance fund, the fund from which we pay benefits to hundreds of thousands of unemployed. When unemployment insurance benefits run out, the taxpayer is called on to pay for welfare in order to prevent the jobless from starving.
My party has calculated that last year unemployment cost each taxpayer an average of $264 extra. The calculation took into account revenue which would have been paid as income tax but was not-since the unemployed do not pay income tax-extra money paid into the unemployment insurance fund and the loss to the economy from lost production. In the face of this, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) has the gall to stand in this House and say that we cannot afford to stimulate the economy, we cannot put Canadians back to work because that would create another inflationary cycle. So far as the Liberal government is concerned, inflation, not unemployment, is the number one problem. That is utter nonsense.
The Minister of Finance well knows that the Canadian economy is operating at only 85 per cent of capacity, that there is slack in the economy, and that if measures are taken to stimulate the economy, to stimulate consumer demand which will lead to increased employment for Canadians, the result will not be another round of inflation. At present we have a situation of massive unemployment which is being met, it seems to me, with massive indifference on the part of the government and to a large extent on the part of the Canadian population.
A thinking Canadian must ask himself, why has the government year after year tolerated such high unemployment? In a country as industrially advanced as Canada, possessing natural resources and abundant human resources in the form of talented working people, why should there be persistently high levels of unemployment? The answer in part to that question must lie within the capitalist system and how it operates. Our free enterprise or capitalist system has within it certain built-in biases which say that high unemployment is not only necessary but tolerable. I came across an article written by Professor Robert Lekachman of the Herbert Lehman College, City University, New York, which was published in this month's Harper's magazine. In it he wrestles with this very question; what, within our economic system, allows the existence year
February 25, 1977

after year of high unemployment? I will read part of his analysis. He said:
The brutal fact is that unemployment at "moderate" rates confers a good many benefits upon the prosperous and the truly affluent. If everyone could be employed, extraordinarily high wages would have to be paid to toilers in restaurant kitchens, laundries, filling stations, and other humble positions. Whenever decent jobs at living wages are plentiful, it is exceedingly difficult to coax young men and women into our volunteer army. Without a volunteer army, how can the children of the middle and upper classes be spared the rigours of the draft?
Unemployment calms the unions and moderates their wage demands. Business periodicals have been noting with unconcealed gratification that last year's contract settlements between major unions and large corporations were considerably less expensive for employers than those of 1975, even though union members were steadily losing ground to inflation. When people are scared about losing their jobs, they work harder and gripe less. In more dignified language, absenteeism declines and productivity ascends.
Better still, factory and office workers, alert to potential layoffs and plant shutdowns, are unlikely to nag unions and employers to make work more interesting, and less menacing to health and personal safety. It cannot be mere coincidence that in Sweden, where job enrichment and plant democracy have had their greatest success, unemployment is practically zero and astute management of their economy protected Swedes even from the world-wide economic crisis of 1973-75. The new government, elected on the fortuitous issue of nuclear safety, has promised to extend even further the social benefits for which Sweden has become celebrated. American employers preserve themselves from Swedish experiments in good part by keeping the industrial reserve army plentifully manned.
Nor is this quite the end of the tale. The hunger of communities and regions for jobs and tax revenues has allowed large corporations to extort an endless assortment of valuable concessions from local and state governments, either as blackmail to keep existing installations or bribes to lure new ones. Few major corporations pay their fair share of property taxes. Propaganda by oil, steel, chemical, and paper industries has noticeably slowed the pace of regulation to protect the environment.
I commend the reading of the article to all members of the House. The professor pointed out that in the capitalist system unemployment is a benefit. As long as there is massive unemployment, the demands of workers who, after all, produce the goods and make the profits for the company, will be moderate. They will keep down their demands for wages and good working conditions. Of course, corporations can pretty well state the conditions on which they will enter into an industry. The only way of narrowing the gap between rich and poor is for a full employment program. That, of course, is a threat to the status quo of those who have a privileged economic position in our society.
[DOT] (M50)
In a sense, this analysis of the contradictions in the capitalist system and why unemployment is at high levels explains why this Liberal government or any future Conservative government are limited in what they can do in coming to grips with the problem of unemployment. They will never restructure the capitalist system and the way it operates. That, of course, would challenge the status quo, the very powerful business elite in our country. The options open to them are reduced to tinkering with the system. We have ample evidence of that kind of tinkering.
The temporary job programs such as the Local Initiatives Program, Opportunities for Youth, and the new fancy ones,
Employment and Immigration
Canada Works and Young Canada Works, and the hand-outs of millions of dollars through the departments of Regional Economic Expansion, and Industry, Trade and Commerce to induce business to locate in an area or expand really never comes to grips with the fundamental contradiction in our present economic system, namely, that if you have full employment, you begin to threaten the status quo, those who have wealth and power. Until we have the option of a party such as the New Democratic Party, which is willing to challenge the powerful corporate elite in our economic system, we will never have more than temporary tinkering measures with regard to job-creation from either the Liberals or the Conservatives.
The second reason we have had perpetually high unemployment surely lies with the degree of foreign ownership in this country. For example, over 90 per cent of our oil industry and over 60 per cent of our manufacturing industry is foreign-owned. Therefore, decisions as to expansion of branch plants or location of subsidiaries lies beyond the control of the Canadian economy. It rests with the decision-makers of the parent company outside Canada. If there is a slowdown in the economy of the United States, obviously it is to the advantage of the parent company to lay off workers in Canadian branch plants before workers in the parent company in the United States. Unless we come to grips with what foreign ownership is doing to our economy in terms of downplaying the creation of the manufacturing industry, which of course is job-intensive, and enhance resource exploitation, we will continue to have high unemployment.
There are always more jobs created in processing raw materials than in taking the raw materials out of the ground, yet our economy has been locked into a continental structure whereby Canadians are still the hewers of wood and drawers of water. We are still the ones who take the minerals, oil and natural gas out of the ground and export them to the United States and elsewhere. In return, we import manufactured goods. We import more than 70 per cent of our manufactured goods from the United States, paying for them with Canadian dollars. The only way we can get back Canadian dollars to help solve our balance of payments problem is to export more and more raw material such as oil and natural gas to the United States. That, of course, is one of the reasons for the great pressure to build the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. If we want to create jobs, we have to regain control of the Canadian economy so that it will be receptive to direction from the Canadian government in terms of creating a national job-creation plan. Neither the Liberal party nor the Conservative party is in any way serious about regaining control of our economy for that purpose.
We will continue to have unemployment as long as we have Liberals and Conservatives managing, because of the existence of the capitalist system. They cannot challenge it or restructure it. Therefore, they are limited to job-tinkering programs and doing what we see before us today in Bill C-27. As the number of unemployed increases, because of the contradictions I have outlined the cost of paying unemployment insurance premiums increases. It has come to the point where it is so
80010-121/2

February 25, 1977
Employment and Immigration
embarrassing in terms of the billions of dollars being paid out in unemployment insurance funds that, quite naturally, this government takes up the only other option open to it. Rather than create jobs, they begin to tighten up on those who are receiving benefits from the unemployment insurance scheme. Therefore, we see in Bill C-27 a list of provisions designed to cut people off the unemployment insurance roll in order to reduce the cost of that program and be able to say to the Canadian taxpayer "what good boys are we."
Let us look at some of the implications of the legislation before us. This legislation flies in the face of the whole reason for an unemployment insurance program in the first place. The basic reason is to ensure workers against the day when they become unemployed. If a fundamental precept of the program is that a worker has the right to be insured against the calamity of unemployment, how does this government justify taking that right away from workers? We often hear people complain about the unemployment insurance scheme. However, they forget that putting money in the hands of the unemployed helps keep the economy going. These people have to buy food for their families from the corner grocery, the farmer and all down the line. It keeps other Canadians employed.
What are the arguments this government puts forward to say that we can afford to throw people off the unemployment insurance rolls? The evidence soon becomes apparent when we look at the clause of the bill which provides that they will have to redefine the entrance requirement or qualification period in order to become eligible for unemployment insurance benefits. Until now, if a worker works eight weeks within a 52-week period and becomes unemployed, he is eligible to receive benefits. This government, despite the record unemployment we have today, wants to raise the qualification period from eight to 12 weeks. This will remove some 330,000 people a year from the unemployment insurance rolls. It is really the old principle of robbing Peter to pay Paul. If people are taken off the unemployment insurance rolls and they cannot find work, they have to go on city on provincial welfare, and the taxpayers end up paying anyway. But this government does not look at the consequences; it is trying to protect its own political hide by this change in the qualifying period.
What is this going to mean to certain regions of the country? It seems to me that the requirement of 12 weeks employment instead of eight weeks to qualify for unemployment insurance is going to discriminate against people in poorer areas of the country which have been suffering severe economic hardship and high unemployment for years. I think particularly of Atlantic Canada, Quebec, and some northern regions, especially my own area of northern Ontario.
When we realize that in the province of Newfoundland, for example, 48 per cent of those who are receiving unemployment insurance benefits had less than 20 weeks' work, the implications of this change to the Unemployment Insurance Act have got to be severe. My leader and I, and a few others of our

caucus, recently travelled to Atlantic Canada to witness firsthand the problems of the unemployed. We heard stories about how it was impossible for them to get work in a fish factory for 12 weeks or more; often all they could get was temporary work. Yet the government ignores this kind of economic reality and proposes to increase the qualifying period for unemployment insurance. The jobs are just not there on a long term basis, and until they are it seems to me that this kind of amendment does not make sense.
The Minister of Manpower likes to say, "Well, we are not really after those who are serious about looking for employment; we are making this change to discourage young people, housewives and others, who are not really dependent upon the extra income to keep the family going but who just want to supplement the family income to raise their standard of living. Really women and young people do not count; we can afford to take them out of the unemployment insurance scheme."
Let us examine the actuality of the situation. Is it true that women and young people who fall into this category are from upper and middle class families and do not really need to work, and so we can afford to take them off the unemployment insurance rolls? Do they just want to work for eight weeks, quit, and then collect their benefits? Let us see what the situation is according to figures issued by the minister's own department and Statistics Canada. Here are some facts on the disentitlement of those who work from eight to 11 weeks. What kind of people are they who are now going to be cut off? We find that in the first five months of 1976 those who worked from eight to 11 weeks, the eight to 11 weekers, made up only 15 per cent of all those in receipt of unemployment insurance benefits. The way the government talks, great numbers are abusing the system, but the government's own statistics reveal that only 15 per cent of the recipients are in this category.
In the first five months of 1976, 63.8 per cent of all eight to 11 weekers were in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces, areas which just do not have long-term work available. The minister keeps telling us, and the media have swallowed the bait, that by eliminating the eight weekers it will be mostly women who will be removed from the unemployment insurance rolls. What are the facts? The facts are that more men, some 214,000, compared with 115,000 women, will be affected by this change. The hardest hit sector will be construction, which is virtually a male preserve.
Those who work for only eight weeks basically come from very low income families that desperately need this extra income from part-time jobs, or more hopefully long-term jobs. When they are laid off and become unemployed, their unemployment insurance benefit is crucial to keeping the family above water in terms of paying bills and feeding themselves.
Again to disprove the suggestion that the great proportion of eight weekers are women who really do not need extra income,
1 would point out that in August StatsCan published a study of unemployment in the years 1973 and 1971, and it was discovered that in both those years unemployed wives tended to come from families of low income. For example, in 1973 the unemployment rate for all wives was 13.5 per cent. Of that
February 25, 1977

figure, 21.4 per cent came from families with incomes between $4,000 and $7,000, whereas only 8.6 per cent came from families with incomes over $15,000. The evidence is clear that unemployment among low income families and particularly among low income working women, was the real problem. The wage of these women in the low income groups was crucial to the family budget. A survey of women in the $4,000 to $7,000 group revealed that they contributed 22 per cent of the family income, whereas women in the $15,000 category contributed only about 17 per cent.
This legislation to change the qualifying period does not make sense. It will continue to discriminate against the poorer regions of the country and poorer families. I think it is disgraceful, in light of the economic calamity that is facing us, for the government to introduce legislation of this kind. There are other examples in the bill of qualifying periods being reduced and of attempts to use some of the unemploymSnt insurance money saved for temporary job training programs, and so on. Some of my hon. friends have gone into this and criticized it. I do not want to do it at this time because my time is running out. I should like in the few minutes remaining to me to put forward some alternative suggestions.
Rather than go after the unemployed and punish them as we are doing under this legislation, why cannot the government prepare and bring forward job-creating programs to get the unemployment rate down to manageable levels? I know it will not come forward with serious programs to challenge and restructure the existing system, but within the framework of the present economic system it could bring forward short-term policies which would help to bring down at least by several hundred thousand this tremendous rate of unemployment.
We in the New Democratic Party have been calling upon the government to bring in personal income tax cuts immediately for low and middle income families to stimulate purchasing power, increase production, and get people back to work. As we have explained, such a move would not create another round of inflation. We have called on the government to reactivate all federal works projects and to encourage the provinces and municipalities to follow suit, at the same time lifting restraints on the shared funding of such projects. This positive approach would get people back to work. Why does the government not take it?
We could have a program, in consultation with the provinces, to expand capital budgets for low income and co-operative housing and land assembly. Today there is a housing crisis. People cannot afford houses. People need houses. The housing industry is one of the most job productive. If we had a massive program to create and build homes we would fulfil an important social need and get Canadians back to work at the same time. We could have a program to upgrade insulation in public buildings and private homes, which would not only conform with the government's stated purpose of conserving energy but also provide employment.
Employment and Immigration
Most important of all, we have to come to grips with the long-term problem of unemployment, and that is the fact that private enterprise has failed to create the jobs needed to keep Canadians employed. It is time the government recognized its democratic responsibility to the electorate. Where private enterprise has failed it has the responsibility to decide, through use of a public investment fund, where private enterprise should expand and locate to get Canadians back to work. We can no longer leave this decision-making process in the hands of private industry most of which is controlled from outside the country.
Sweden has demonstrated most successfully a co-operative program between government and private industry through an investment fund which requires industry to allocate a certain percentage of profits in a central investment fund in return for certain tax advantages. Under such a scheme the investment could only be carried out when and where the government approved in order that we could really stimulate regional economic development, and when the economy went into a decline we would have investment funds to provide the necessary new capital to get Canadians back to work. However, as I said, I do not see the Liberals or the Conservatives tackling the long-range weaknesses of our economy.
I hope that the government at least will have the good sense to listen to some of the proposals I have put forward for the short-term, proposals it can live with and which will at the same time create jobs. Amending the Unemployment Insurance Act hits the unemployed but does nothing to create jobs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the introduction of Bill C-27 in the House and the debate on second reading prompt me to make to the minister and the government some comments which are often drawn to my attention by my constituents.
Before doing so, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) that I am satisfied with the federal decision which is consistent with the wishes of members as well as their constituents and also adjusted to the speedy development in the employment field, to make, through that bill, some important amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am especially pleased with that progressive and realistic step taken to amalgamate the Manpower Centre with the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Indeed we hope that such an amalgamation will remove any inconvenience for the workers who had to fall from Scylla into Charybdis as they had to seek a job and at the same time apply for unemployment insurance when temporarily out of work.
Hopefully, from now on the unemployed will at least find everything from the same person if not under the same roof. This is truly a realistic and consistent policy. My remarks will bear mostly on the following approaches to Bill C-27 and on the Unemployment Insurance Act in general, on the increased number of working weeks before seeking unemployment insurance benefits, on the eligibility for certain jobs, on the delay of the process taking place between application for and receipt of

February 25, 1977
Employment and Immigration
benefits and, finally, on the abolition of discrimination against the handicapped.
Hon. members will recall that in 1971, after many months of cogitation, continuing the social policy innovated in Canada by the party now in power, the Liberal party-coming to grips with new social requirements and, one must add, inspired by an unfaltering minister-improved the condition of thousands of Canadians who were unemployed because of various factors over which they had no control and, in many instances, who were deprived of unemployment insurance benefits.
The Liberal government of the time decided it was high time to amend the Unemployed Insurance Act. The considerable difference between wages and benefits which existed at that time and which had not changed with the gradual increase in wages, was enough to justify the 1971 revision, aimed at creating a more realistic and fair balance. But the act went further.
In order to guarantee an income to those workers who could count on employment for only a part of the year, and several members have stressed this before me, as was and is still the case in Canada and particularly in my region where the fishery, forest and other industries like tourism are seasonal activities, it was imperative to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. Unfortunately, as almost always happens, experience has shown us, since the enforcement of the act in 1971, that some intolerable abuses have taken place, which the present legislation seeks to correct. The good will have to pay once more for the improper conduct of those of their fellow citizens who, it is sad to say, would rather draw unemployment insurance than work.
On this subject, Mr. Speaker, I would like once again to point out to the minister and other members that available jobs do not have the same diversity and the same permanent aspect in every regions of this country. In the Magdalen Islands, for example, where fishery is the main industry, the islanders are inevitably fishermen or work somehow within this industry. Directly or not, people in the islands live of fishery. When the season is closed, the fishermen or fish processing plant workers cannot be all absorbed by the other sectors of the economy on the islands. What can they do then? Where will those people go to earn a living during the five, six or seven months before the next fishing season?
Those people are not exactly unskilled. Most of them if not nearly all of them can work at other things. Several of them, the luckier, accept to exile themselves and go to work elsewhere when they manage to find a job, but what about the others? They are left with only the unemployment insurance benefits, when they have been able through fishing to accumulate the required number of weeks, or with social welfare allowances. In this respect, Mr. Speaker, the manpower centers scattered thoughout our regions should demonstrate a little more initiative and imagination, and use employment pools other than the sole employment service for available or unemployed labour.

It remains-I am willing to admit this-that even with the best scheme, a number of unemployed could not find a job. In cases such as those which are found in the Magdalen Islands and elsewhere in my constituency, as well as in the Gaspe peninsula generally, including the Gaspe and Matane constituencies, and some neighbouring areas, the whole Restigouche area, the Gloucester area and New Brunswick as a whole, it should be possible, wherever the industrial base is very limited, to adopt special measures, as mentioned by previous speakers, until such a time at least when the government decides to organize the economy in a way which would guarantee a more permanent employment of our active population. Just as the duration of benefits varies and the number of weeks increases depending on the difference between the local or regional rate of unemployment and the national average, so, in my humble opinion, should the number of working weeks before obtaining benefits vary in the case of the Magdalen Islands and the Gaspe peninsula in general, as well as the New Brunswick and the Atlantic provinces ridings. Let us put an end to the ridiculous practice whereby an applicant must file evidence that he is looking for a job in a region such as ours where there are few openings, if any. Instead we should require all employers to report job openings to Canada manpower offices, including those they fill themselves without going through the manpower centres. This way manpower officials will always know what jobs are available.
Another serious problem, Mr. Speaker, particularly in our rural regions, is the plight of workers who earn their living by doing little jobs here and there for their neighbour which is not a contractor. For example, let us imagine a good citizen of the Bonaventure riding called Arthur who is a carpenter. His neighbour Alphonse asks for his help to build his house; he cannot afford to complete it all at once so he is building in stages. Alphonse or Gaston keeps Arthur busy for one month with this job. As required by the law, the employer, Alphonse, has deducted from Arthur's wages the federal and provincial income tax, the unemployment insurance and pension plan contributions. Two days after Arthur has finished working for Alphonse, Gaston asks him to work for him. Arthur is a good carpenter and Gaston has decided to have his basement finished. So Arthur works for Gaston one month and a half, until the month of December.
Both employers have deducted all the marginal benefits. But at the end of December, Arthur is unemployed. When you have no job, you are supposed to be unemployed. So Arthur applies for unemployment insurance at the nearest UIC office. His employer gave him the forms relating to the employment termination. And what is the result of his application? Well, the UIC refuses to pay the benefits. For what reason? It is most unfortunate, but the period during which Arthur worked for his neighbours Gaston, Alphonse or Romeo does not count for unemployment insurance purposes as far as the Department of National Revenue is concerned.
I now have to deal with a case the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) is looking into; I hope it will not take her too long to solve it-although it has already dragged on
February 25, 1977

quite some time-and solve it in favour of the party concerned, before he dies. The employer, in this case, as required by law in the province of Quebec, did obtain his contractor's permit, if you please, but did not get an unemployment insurance number allowing him to give stamps to his employee. He did, however, take the precaution of getting a contractor's permit from the provincial government before starting to build his house, because that is what he was building. And so, as provided by law, this employer, this individual, on the strength of a contractor's permit, deducted all the marginal benefits: unemployment insurance, taxes, etc, and they are many! Despite that, his employee has been refused unemployment benefits since December. I find that totally unfair and intolerable. In addition, what about the people who happen to be relatives of an employer? I confess that in this case there can be abuse, but it does seem to me, Mr. Speaker, that today accounting procedures are easy enough to check without having to go through all kinds of investigations and ridiculous annoyances.
That reminds me also, Mr. Speaker-and I do not know whether or not you have lived with that kind of situation in Ontario but we did and we are still living with it in Quebec- how ridiculous are those who insisted and still insist that persons seeking social assistance get rid of their cows or their garden before becoming entitled to social welfare, or those intelligent social workers who suggest that couples separate to get more financial help.
I say that such middle-ages machiavelism and tortures must come to an end. Such practices are immoral and unworthy of a civilized society like ours. I urge the minister, the cabinet and the government to take at once the necessary corrective measures. I do not want to generalize when I mention the unbending and distorted feelings which inspire certain officials either in Quebec, in the federal government or at all government levels, but some of them would feel more at home with Idi Amin Dada's cohorts.
I would also like to point out how long it takes, in some cases, to settle benefit claims. I admit that to err is human and that, as Jean-Jacques Rousseau said, "as long as they are human beings, there is human failure", but I refuse to think that everyone is dishonest and lazy. Yet, it is a computer which carries out most of these operations during this process. Is the electronic brain to be blamed? If I take as a basis the argument so often used to answer our recriminations and our unremitting demands, it is this computer which is responsible for most of these delays. Should we come back to manual processing? As strange as it may appear, there were fewer mistakes and less delay when the UIC did not use the computer. You would not have me believe, for example, that, concerning the general construction strike last summer in the province of Quebec, it was not possible to come to a decision before December.
I should say to conclude how pleased I am-not on these matters-but to see that the department is finally admitting that there is discrimination on the ground of physical hand-
Employment and Immigration
icap. Nothing is more stupefying than to see the contempt some employers show for people less endowed by nature or who have been incapacitated by illness or accident which, without preventing them from working, reduced their abilities and is considered as a handicap by these employers, when they come to ask for a job.
I have in mind an outrageous case in the riding of Bonaven-ture-Iles-de-la-Madeleine, the one of a man built like an athlete, a very hard worker able to squash the army of whipper-snappers who reject him with the back of the hand because he is a diabetic. This man is Mr. William Sawyer from New Carlisle. The Canadian National Railways deny him a job because of his diabetes. This man, who always was a construction worker, or something hard like that, wanted more security so he applied to the Canadian National Railways. Of course these days one might wonder just how much security there is working for the CNR. But in any event, he was required by the company doctor to pass the usual examinations, including the check-up. He was hired and went to work, doing his job without any trouble for about two weeks. His was operating a drilling machine. Without further ado coming back from work after 15 days he was dismissed because of his illness. Another doctor of the Canadian National Railways had considered him unfit for that work, unlike the first doctor, and on the report of the first doctor who had sent him to work.
That, Mr. Speaker, is revolting when the Canadian Diabetes Association has proven that a person suffering from that disease who follows his doctor's instructions on his particular case can normally go about his business without danger. Above all, let the CN not use passenger safety as the pretense for dismissing Mr. Sawyer. So I say bravo to the minister for taking that discrimination out of the legislation, and I hope that the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the government will do their duty and bring that Crown corporation to reason, and that it will correct that injustice against a Canadian by rehiring him immediately.
Mr. Speaker, those are the reflections I felt I had to make on this bill, as well as the Unemployment Insurance Act, and certain anomalies in its application, and particularly on many injustices and worries resulting therefrom. Let us give our future Canadian Employment and Immigration Commission offices the necessary staff and tools to function not like a body without soul working in the cold regions of pure civil service but with a soul filled with the desire to fulfill a humanitarian task, a soul and a heart vibrating in harmony with those of their fellow citizens in whose employ their work and the government have placed them.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so that we might be reminded of the scope of the measure we are currently debating, I would like to read once again its description. It is, and I quote:
... to establish the Department of Employment and Immigration, the Canada Employment and Immigration Commission and the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof.

February 25, 1977
Employment and Immigration
I realize that the unemployment insurance aspect of this bill is one of the most important aspects contained in it. I believe that underlines once again one of the most persistent and, at this point in time, one of the most urgent problems confronting the nation, and that is, of course, the problem of unemployment.
Since returning to this House in 1972 after a period of rest and recuperation, I have noted that each budget address has included in its state of the nation resume a statement to the effect that unemployment is one of the most pressing problems, that the government is dedicating its energies to its solution, and that it is going to take remedial action to overcome it.
However, I suggest that through the failure of the government to take effective action, principally because it is unable to understand the problem-let alone take remedial action- the prospects for the coming months are rather bleak indeed. Once again we are faced with a series of patchwork programs which, unless they break out of the circle of failures which befell their predecessors, will do little to inspire confidence or hope for the future of Canada.
When the government recessed parliament for Christmas on December 21, 1976, no doubt it hoped that the intervening 32 days would bring some improvement to the economic situation facing Canada. Throughout the fall session the government consistently evaded opposition questions about the economy. It stalled on taking any effective action to remedy the sickness which was afflicting our nation during that period, and which continues to afflict it today. Then in a hastily put-together package the government announced make-work programs such as Canada Works, which really seemed-and I think this is proving to be the case-to spend money, while giving only the appearance of remedial action as far as unemployment is concerned.
I would like to make it quite clear today that I am taking part in the Canada Works program by nominating persons to the minister for appointment to the ministerial advisory board. I do not, however, have very much confidence that the minister really knows what he is doing, other than spending a great amount of taxpayers' money. I hope I am wrong, but the program was thrown together too quickly, the deadline for applications came too quickly, and as my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), pointed out when speaking in this debate, some parts of the nation had the application forms while other parts did not.
It seems to me that this is very haphazard way of trying to implement a program which was designed specifically to meet the problem of chronic unemployment we are facing at the present time. When this matter was brought to the attention of the minister and it was suggested that the deadline be extended, he decline to extend it until after the expiry date, and then he pointed out that the government had agreed to let it go for another week. Of course this was completely useless because those who were not able to file by the deadline took it for granted that that was the end of the matter and they did not have time to process applications to meet the new deadline
that had been established. It seems to me there must be some more consistent and deliberate attention given to programs if they are to serve their purposes to the ultimate degree.
Now we are faced with the very serious problem of unemployment in Canada. After the Christmas recess we expected the government to be ready to move ahead with a program of business. The first item on the government's list of priorities, however, was a resolution dealing with televising the proceedings of this House. Mr. Speaker, I do not think any substantial percentage of the people of this country worry whether the proceedings of this House are televised or not. Personally, and I know others have attested to the same thing, I believe there is absolutely no indication that the people are interested in it. But when we had a national unemployment rate approaching 8 per cent-or 12 per cent- the government wanted to debate televising the proceedings of this House.
The next resolution to come before us concerned metric conversion, something of minor importance in comparison to the other problems facing Canada. How the government can establish such a set of priorities and expect to maintain credibility with the people of Canada is beyond my comprehension.
To top it all, when my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton West, led off the questioning on the first day back by asking the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if he would make a state of the nation type of address outlining the problems facing the country in the areas of unemployment and inflation, and announce the government's initiatives to improve the situation, he was met with what can only be termed a total abdication of leadership. The question was turned over to a parliamentary secretary for reply.
Later in that same question period the Prime Minister condescended to answer a supplementary question and stated that when and if such an announcement were made it would be in a budget speech by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). While this country was facing the three most serious problems any country could face, the government was playing games and not facing up to the problems which required its leadership and direction.
It would have been reasonable to expect that during the Christmas recess of 32 days the government would have met with its economic advisers to formulate a plan to pull the country out of the recessionary trend with which we were faced. Instead, the government took the time of the House to debate issues of relatively minor importance.
One of the most reliable economic forecasting agencies, the Conference Board in Canada, predicted during the middle of January that economic growth in Canada's two most populous and heavily industrialized provinces, Ontario and Quebec, will slacken this year to "drag national production downward and significantly raise unemployment". The board went on to say that the nation's economic situation was considerably less optimistic looking than it had appeared in the fall, and predicted real growth in Canadian output would decline to 3 per cent

February 25, 1977

from last year's 5 per cent "unless the government took action to stimulate the economy".
The board went on to say:
The outlooks for spending on capital goods, consumer goods and housing have all been revised downward since the fall and this is reflected in the projections of total output in manufacturing and construction industries in the year 1977.
Since these industries play a relatively greater role in the economies of Ontario and Quebec, one can readily see the outlook for growth in these provinces is considerably less favourable than it was in the fall.
As we think of the situation across the country, the growth rate in Saskatchewan is expected to be the nation's worst with a predicted production decline of 0.8 per cent. The unemployment rate in Newfoundland-and this has been vividly brought to our attention by my colleagues in this debate-is anything but bright; in fact it is catastrophic.
At the same time as the Conference Board in Canada was making its economic predictions, analysts reported to the Toronto Dominion Bank that "only additional stimulus will improve Canada's economic performance in 1977 but the trends are not good". In its winter issue of "Canada's Business Climate", the bank's economists suggest:
Real growth in the economy will remain weak, advancing only 4 per cent. Prices should moderate slightly but unemployment will average l/i per cent.
From every angle then, we can see that the nation is facing declining production and increasing unemployment. In fact among Canada's foremost economic forecasting organizations only one has predicted an economic improvement in the months ahead, and that is the Economic Council of Canada- an offspring of the federal government. All the rest, including the Conference Board in Canada, the chartered banks and the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, have warned of deteriorating conditions.
There is a desperate need in the country for some economic leadership. The government has passed the buck, has blamed everyone but itself for the situation that has evolved. We have stated many times in the past and we reiterate that the government's own spending habits have contributed more to the inflationary spiral than any other single factor. Its mismanagement in other economic areas has been documented and stated clearly in this House on many occasions. It is little wonder that, as far as the popularity of the government is concerned, it is at a very low level right across the nation.
For several months now the leader of my party has been advocating some of the measures he believed in and was advancing in order to meet the challenge of these days in which we live. He advocated an immediate tax cut in personal income tax as a stimulus to the economy. The government has consistently refused to agree that this measure would be desirable and effective. In the meantime investment capital is continuing to flow out of Canada because of social and political uncertainty, but most of all because of economic uncertainty created by the government. Economic experts claim that this uncertain climate for business means that Canadian money as well will continue to flow out of the country. This Canadian money should remain here and be available for
Employment and Immigration
Canadian entrepreneurial activity. We have a situation where Canadian money is being invested outside Canada while foreign investors are reducing or curtailing their direct investment here.
The Minister of Finance addressed the Canadian Club of Toronto some weeks ago. He said:
There is no question that we need a progressive recovery in private investment if we are going to be able to provide adequately for job creation and rising productivity . .. The control of profit margins has been no tonic for investment ... We recognize that fact.
I must say that the minister does not seem to believe what he was saying, nor do I believe that the government is really interested in fostering a positive climate for business.
I listened with a great deal of interest to our friend from the New Democratic Party extolling the philosophy that his party espouses. He talked about the failure of private enterprise to meet the challenge of these days. I should like to remind him that I live in the province of British Columbia, and when the New Democratic Party formed the government there they certainly did not introduce any Utopia. We would not look forward to a return of that government, although there is no possibility of it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: Nonsense.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: It seems to me that the hon. member's party has a tenuous hold on power in those other provinces presently governed by an NDP government, but after the next provincial elections they will be in the backwoods.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext: In Manitoba, too.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ESTABLISH DEPARTMENT OF EMPLOYMENT AND IMMIGRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, in Manitoba and in the other provinces where the hon. member's party forms a government. The hon. member need not think he is putting anything over; he is not fooling us. We are not naive enough to accept his kind of argument. We know what the NDP's philosophy is, and what happens when it is applied.
I alluded to the Canada Works program earlier. I think these make-work programs serve as a good illustration for what I was saying about the government's real attitude about private enterprise. The need for make-work programs is based on government policies that have failed to create the economic climate in which private enterprise could flourish, produce goods, and provide services, thereby providing the job opportunities required for our work force. Make-work programs like Canada Works or Young Canada Works become necessary when the government, rather than encouraging and assisting personal initiative and enterprise, strangles private enterprise and makes it incapable of fulfilling its economic and social role in society.
The throne speech which opened this second session of the Thirtieth Parliament made mention of "improving the efficiency of the labour market and actively hastening the return of unemployed workers to productive effort." That sounds great. It has a nice ring to it, just like "the just society" or "the land

February 25, 1977
Employment and Immigration
is strong." This government has a way of coining beautiful phrases; unfortunately they are not reflected in any of the programs or policies the government brings forward.
The government, while talking about returning unemployed workers to productive effort, is led by a man who just a few short years ago told the people of Canada that his concept of the work ethic was that if anyone did not want to work, he should not have to work; the inference to be drawn was that it was the responsibility of society to make certain that those who do not want to work have sufficient cash on which to live, without making any constructive contribution to society.
When we compare the Prime Minister's attitude with that demonstrated by the Minister of Finance when the latter talked to the Canadian Club in Toronto, we find that there is a large credibility gap. The minister claimed in that speech that he knows the problem. What solutions did he propose? He failed to propose remedies. All he gave us was simply more government rhetoric. That was as far as he went. The theory of the government appears to be that if you talk enough about a problem, surround the discussion with enough statistics and wait long enough, the problem will go away. This bill deals with one of the problems created by unemployment. If we are to meet the problem envisaged in the bill and resolve it, the government will need to be more constructive and take greater initiatives.
A recent report of the Economic Council of Canada entitled "Jobs and People" found that the Prime Minister's attitude is reflected in the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The report documents that "the structure of the unemployment insurance benefits, coupled with the ease of entry into the program"-as a result of the government's lax attitude, I might add-"have combined to undermine the work ethic." As well, recipients are remaining on UIC rolls for increasingly longer periods of time. While the average coverage lasts approximately 15 weeks, the report reveals that 75 per cent of females, and over 65 per cent of males, remain on UIC benefits for over 20 weeks, that is, into the extended benefit period. That is an indictment of the operation of the unemployment insurance program.
According to the report, the disincentive factor built into the operation now accounts for approximately 10 per cent of additional unemployment. Some say that is not much, that we should not complain bitterly about a relatively small figure. But in real terms it means that the 1971 revisions have induced between 60,000 and 70,000 additional Canadians to become unemployed. They are Canadians who otherwise would have been contributing to this nation's productivity. If the government is really serious about improving the efficiency of the labour market and actively hastening the return of unemployed workers to productive effort, as the throne speech states, then this is one area in which it can start acting. As my colleague from Hamilton West said, unemployment insurance should be just that, insurance. It should not be operated as a welfare program.
Our party is committed to a policy of support for small and medium-sized businesses. I have said on other occasions in the

House, and 1 repeat it, that small business in Canada guarantees more employment, more real growth, more tax revenue, and bears more of the cost burden of government than does so-called big business. Small businesses are the backbone of the Canadian business community. They create over 50 per cent of the taxes collected by the government, and employ close to 60 per cent of the people working in Canada.
In the last budget the government expanded its definition of small business by offering more tax reductions. This will help somewhat and we support even this small step because we believe that anything done to encourage the small business sector of the economy will have a positive effect on the employment situation.
I should like to mention a number of proposals which have been emphasized, indeed brought forward on a number of occasions, by members of my party. Our attitude to this serious matter now before the House is not destructive. The issue is too important to warrant the presentation of its darker or bleaker side only. Perhaps on another occasion I shall be given the opportunity to present some of our constructive proposals, Mr. Speaker.
